items.title: Lemon Juice Does Not Cure COVID-19
items.snippet_en: There is no scientific evidence that lemon juice, hot water, or their combination can kill the coronavirus or prevent COVID-19. Viral infections involve viruses entering cells and replicating; lemon juice does not destroy viruses or stop replication. While lemons contain vitamin C, there's no evidence it can "boost" the immune system to protect against coronavirus.

outputs.notes_en: The claim that drinking hot water mixed with lemon juice will destroy the coronavirus is false. Multiple sources, including fact-checking organizations and medical experts, have debunked this claim, stating there is no scientific evidence to support it. There is no data or scientific evidence to suggest that lemon juice, hot water, or a combination of both can kill the coronavirus or prevent COVID-19 infection. One study indicated that the virus can survive in acidic environments, contradicting the idea that lemon juice's acidity would be effective. The pH level inside the human body cannot be significantly changed by consuming lemon water. Viral infections involve viruses entering cells and replicating; lemon juice does not destroy viruses in the body or stop this replication process. While lemons contain vitamin C, there's no evidence that it can "boost" the immune system to protect against coronavirus infections. This claim was part of widespread misinformation and "quack cures" that circulated online during the pandemic. Organizations like the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have stated that there is no specific medicine recommended to prevent or treat the new coronavirus and emphasize practices like handwashing, mask-wearing, and social distancing. While some sources mention drinking warm water with lemon and ginger as a home remedy for general hydration and to support the immune system during illness, they do not claim it cures or destroys the coronavirus.
